\section[nox]{nox — English's own word, wearing a Roman toga}

\label{lesson:LA-C29-nox}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Last lesson gave \emph{diēs} its own moment. Here's its partner from \emph{media nox} — and this time, the English cousin isn't hiding behind centuries of sound change. It's staring you in the face.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nox — "night"}
\textbf{Nox} (genitive \textbf{noctis}) — "\textbf{night}" — is the word you've already met inside \textbf{media nox} ("midnight," Chapter 12).

\begin{cousinweb}
Trace \emph{nox} back far enough and you land on \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*nók\textsuperscript{w}ts}} — and this is about as solid a reconstruction as historical linguistics gets. The cognates read almost like the same word spelled differently across a dozen languages: English's own \textbf{night}, German \textbf{Nacht}, Greek \textbf{nyx}, Sanskrit \textbf{nakta}, Old Norse \textbf{nátt}, Gothic \textbf{nahts}. \emph{Nox} and "night" aren't just related — they're about as close to being the same word as two languages 6,000 years apart can get.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: The same suffix as diurnum, and a name for equal nights}]
Nox's own derivative, \textbf{nocturnus} ("of the night"), wasn't built from scratch — it was coined \textbf{directly on the analogy} of \emph{diēs}'s own \textbf{diurnum}, reusing its exact \emph{-urnus} suffix on purpose: the same suffix-machine, deliberately applied to a second time-word. \emph{Nocturnus} gives English \textbf{nocturnal} and \textbf{nocturne} directly. And \textbf{aequus} ("equal") + nox's stem \emph{noct-} gives \textbf{equinox} — literally "\textbf{equal night}," the day when day and night balance.
\end{grammarlens}
